solutions.explanation:
The reciprocal requires \(r\ne0\). If complex values of \(r\) are permitted, expand the given square to obtain
\[
r^2+2+\frac1{r^2}=3,
\qquad r^2+\frac1{r^2}=1.
\]
The sum-of-cubes identity is useful because the two quantities \(r\) and \(1/r\) have product \(1\). It gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
r^3+\frac1{r^3}
&=\left(r+\frac1r\right)
  \left(r^2-1+\frac1{r^2}\right)\\
&=\left(r+\frac1r\right)(1-1)=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, under the complex-number interpretation, the answer is \(\boxed{0}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

There is a domain issue if \(r\) is intended to be real. The same hypothesis would imply
\[
\left(r-\frac1r\right)^2
=r^2-2+\frac1{r^2}
=1-2=-1.
\]
A real square cannot be negative, so no real \(r\) satisfies the condition. Consequently, choice C is the intended algebraic value when complex numbers are allowed; over the reals, the stated situation cannot occur.
solutions.title: Factor the sum of cubes and check the domain
